reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Classically follows an episode of forceful vomiting or retching, often after a large meal or alcohol, and presents with sudden severe chest or upper abdominal pain
The Mackler triad of vomiting, chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema is characteristic but present in only a minority of patients
The rupture usually occurs in the distal left posterolateral oesophagus, which typically produces a left-sided pleural effusion and hydropneumothorax
Subcutaneous or mediastinal emphysema may be detected clinically or on imaging, and mediastinitis develops rapidly
It is distinguished from the mucosal tear of a Mallory-Weiss lesion by being a full-thickness (transmural) rupture
Water-soluble contrast oesophagography or CT confirms the leak and localises the perforation
Management is a surgical emergency, with surgical repair for Boerhaave alongside drainage, broad-spectrum antibiotics and nutritional support, and endoscopic options in selected cases
reference.pathophysiology: Boerhaave syndrome is a spontaneous full-thickness rupture of the oesophagus caused by a sudden rise in intraluminal pressure against a closed upper oesophageal sphincter, typically during forceful vomiting or retching. The pressure surge tears the wall, usually at the weaker distal left posterolateral segment. Gastric and oral contents then contaminate the mediastinum and, because the rupture communicates with the left pleural cavity, frequently the left pleural space, provoking a fulminant chemical and bacterial mediastinitis and pleuritis with sepsis. The condition is distinct from iatrogenic perforation and from the partial-thickness mucosal tears of Mallory-Weiss syndrome.
additionalInvestigations: Water-soluble contrast oesophagogram to demonstrate the leak
CT of the chest and abdomen to show mediastinal air, fluid and pleural effusion
Chest radiograph looking for pneumomediastinum, effusion and hydropneumothorax
Pleural fluid analysis, which may show food debris, low pH or raised amylase
Baseline bloods and lactate to assess sepsis and physiological status
redFlags: Sepsis or septic shock from mediastinitis
Rapidly enlarging pleural effusion or tension hydropneumothorax
Delayed presentation with established mediastinal contamination
Haemodynamic instability requiring urgent resuscitation and surgery
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends critically on time to diagnosis and treatment; early intervention gives reasonable survival, whereas delay beyond about a day markedly increases mortality from mediastinitis and sepsis.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as a cardiac, aortic or pulmonary emergency and delaying treatment
Confusing it with the mucosal Mallory-Weiss tear and underestimating severity
Using barium rather than water-soluble contrast when perforation is suspected
Underestimating fluid and antibiotic needs in a septic patient
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Urgent surgical repair of the transmural rupture (primary repair over drainage) as definitive treatment, with endoscopic stenting or clipping and drainage reserved for selected contained or late-presenting cases
Immediate resuscitation with nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics plus antifungal cover, and a proton pump inhibitor
Drainage of mediastinal and pleural contamination, including chest-drain placement for the pleural collection
Nutritional support via feeding jejunostomy or parenteral nutrition while the oesophagus heals
Critical-care support with aggressive management of mediastinitis and sepsis
Emergency upper-gastrointestinal or thoracic surgical referral, recognising that survival falls sharply with delayed diagnosis and treatment
